investigacion.base:
Need week 40 and 41.**Status: no figure yet.** The Week 42 report has not been published (it's expected around Oct 29). Neither has Week 41, which should come out around Oct 22. The latest official number is **368** from Week 40. Today is Oct 19, 2026.

**What the cited sources say**
- **Week 40 report (Oct 4–10, the latest):** "In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported". That's in Broward, Hillsborough (310), Miami-Dade (9), Orange (5), Palm Beach, Pasco (4), Pinellas (37), and Polk. Seventy-two cases of locally acquired dengue were reported this week. This was the biggest weekly jump so far, and 368 is the same number used as the example in the question.
- **Week 42 PDF:** not published yet.
- **Metaculus FAQ:** only defines what counts as a "credible source." It contains no data.

**Weekly totals from FDOH reports**
| Week (ending) | Total so far | Added that week |
|---|---|---|
| W29 (Jul 25) | 1 | 1 |
| W30 (Aug 1) | 4 | 3 |
| W33 (Aug 22) | 41 | — |
| W35 (Sep 5) | 111 | 38 |
| W36 (Sep 12) | 152 (news reports) | ~41 |
| W37 (Sep 19) | 190 | ~38 |
| W38 (Sep 26) | 252 | 62 |
| W39 (Oct 3) | 296 | 44 |
| W40 (Oct 10) | 368 | 72 |

Over the last five weeks, between 38 and 72 cases were added each week, averaging about 51. Two more reports (Weeks 41 and 42) are due before the question resolves. If that pace holds, the Week 42 total would land around 460–520. A Week 42 report adding about 72 cases, like Week 40, would put it near 510. If cases speed up, the total could go above 520. If they slow down, it could stay below 450. This is a simple extrapolation, not a forecast.

**Context and what's driving the numbers**
- **Where cases are:** most of the outbreak is in Tampa Bay and is almost entirely DENV-2. Pinellas is growing fast: Pinellas has 37 locally acquired cases, a week after reporting 20. Hillsborough and Pinellas were extending a local state of emergency covering dengue until Oct. 22. A new locally acquired case in Brevard County was reported around Oct 18. It's unclear whether it will show up in the Week 41 count.
- **Reporting delays:** Weekly jumps do not equal new infections that week. For example, some cases added in Week 39 had symptoms that began in August. Because cases are reported late, totals can keep climbing for several weeks even if transmission slows. Cooler weather tends to slow transmission, but the effect shows up in the reports with a delay.
- **Historical comparison:** 2025, when Florida reported just 62 cases for the entire year. In 2024 there were 91 cases. In 2023 there were 186, which was the previous recent high. State reports and medical literature suggest Florida's 2026 outbreak is the largest calendar-year total for any mainland U.S. state since at least the 1940s.

**Upcoming dates**
- Around Oct 22: Week 41 report. This is the key data point to check.
- Oct 22: the current Hillsborough and Pinellas emergency orders expire.
- Around Oct 29: Week 42 report, which decides the question. If it isn't out, the fallback is the latest report published by Oct 30, which would probably be Week 41.

I didn't find any prediction-market prices for this question.

criterios: This question resolves to the cumulative number of 2026 locally acquired ("Dengue Cases Acquired in Florida") dengue cases reported in the Florida Department of Health (FDOH) Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report for Week 42 of 2026 (the week ending October 24, 2026), expected to be published on or around October 29, 2026 at https://www.floridahealth.gov/statistics-data/population-surveillance/arbovirus-surveillance/ (direct PDF expected at https://www.floridahealth.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/fl-arbovirus-report-w42-2026.pdf). The resolving figure is the single year-to-date total stated in the "2026 Dengue Cases Acquired in Florida" section (e.g., the report stating "In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported" resolves as 368). If the Week 42 report is not available, the most recent Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report published on or before October 30, 2026 (and dated after the Week 40 report) will be used instead.
letra_pequena: Only the year-to-date cumulative count of locally acquired (in-state mosquito-transmitted) dengue cases counts; international travel-associated dengue cases are excluded. If FDOH revises the cumulative total in the resolving report relative to prior weeks, the figure printed in the resolving report governs. If no qualifying report is published anywhere by October 30, 2026 and the figure cannot be determined from [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions), the question is annulled.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About 10 days until the expected Week 42 report on October 29, 2026.

(b) **If nothing changed:** The latest published cumulative total would remain 368 cases.

(c) **If the recent trend continued:** Two more weekly additions near the recent average of about 51 would bring the total to roughly 470. Repeating Week 40’s larger addition of 72 twice would bring it to 512.

(d) **Experts and markets:** The research provides no expert numerical forecast or usable prediction-market estimate. The recent FDOH reports are the strongest guide.

(e) **Unexpected low outcome:** A sharp slowdown in reported additions, or a reporting delay, could leave the total near 400.

(f) **Unexpected high outcome:** Faster spread outside Hillsborough combined with a backlog of cases being reported could push the total above 600.

(a) **Time left:** The Week 42 report should come out around October 29, about 10 days from now. The Week 41 report, due around October 22, will be an important intermediate data point.

(b) **If nothing changed:** The total would stay at 368. That is not realistic, because the report must add two more weeks of cases.

(c) **If the current trend continued:** Over the last six reports, weekly additions were roughly 38, 41, 38, 62, 44 and 72, an average of about 51. The trend is rising, and Pinellas is growing fast (from 20 to 37 cases in one week). Adding two weeks at 50–75 cases each gives about 470–520. My central estimate is around 490.

(d) **Expert and market expectations:** I found no markets on this question. The question creator's likely range is 380–600. Officials are extending emergency orders, which signals that transmission is ongoing. Reporting delays mean the totals will keep rising even if transmission slows in cooler late-October weather.

(e) **Low scenario:** Transmission and reporting slow sharply as temperatures drop and mosquito control takes effect, with about 30 cases added each week. The total would be around 430. Alternatively, the Week 42 report is delayed past October 30, so the question resolves on Week 41 at about 410–440. A downward revision is also possible.

(f) **High scenario:** Pinellas and Hillsborough keep accelerating, a backlog of delayed lab confirmations clears, and new counties such as Brevard add cases. Weekly additions of 90 or more would push the total to about 560–600.

(a) **The time left until the outcome to the question is known:** Approximately 10 to 11 days (the FDOH Week 42 Arbovirus Surveillance Report is expected on Thursday, October 29, 2026, with the resolution window extending to October 30, 2026).
(b) **The outcome if nothing changed:** If no new cases were added to the FDOH report after Week 40, the cumulative total would remain at 368 cases.
(c) **The outcome if the current trend continued:** Over the past 4 to 5 weeks, FDOH has added an average of approximately 50 to 55 locally acquired dengue cases per weekly report (+38, +62, +44, +72). Two additional reports (Weeks 41 and 42) at this average rate of ~54 cases/week would yield ~108 additional cases, bringing the Week 42 cumulative total to approximately 475–480 cases.
(d) **The expectations of experts and markets:** There are no active liquid prediction markets for this specific metric. Epidemic tracking and local mosquito control officials note ongoing multi-county transmission (with Pinellas accelerating and Hillsborough remaining high), making a range between 460 and 520 the baseline expectation for Week 42, with plausible extremes spanning from the 420s to upper 500s.
(e) **An unexpected scenario that results in a low outcome:** Strong mosquito control interventions, rapid clearing of lab testing backlogs, and/or an administrative delay in publishing the Week 42 report by October 30 (triggering resolution via the Week 41 report instead) could result in a total in the low 400s (e.g., 410–435).
(f) **An unexpected scenario that results in a high outcome:** A major surge in retrospective case ascertainment across multiple Tampa Bay and Central Florida counties, coupled with a surge in confirmed lab reports clearing a testing backlog, could add 85–100+ cases in each of Weeks 41 and 42, pushing the Week 42 total beyond 540 cases.
